meta: AI has finished its answer, but it isn't sent yet: it has to pass output guardrails, the gate on the way out. Three checks: does it promise something the policy doesn't allow, does it leak or say anything harmful, does it cite sources.
prompt: Where is this policy written? Please send me the link.

muc.title: Written, but not sent yet
muc.text: AI has finished writing its answer. But it isn't sent right away. It has to pass output guardrails, the gate on the way out.

muc.title: Is it making promises?
muc.text: Check one: does it promise something the policy doesn't allow? As in video 61, an airline had to pay because its chatbot made up a refund policy. Guardrails compare the answer with the policy documents, and strike any line without a source.

muc.title: Leaky, rude, dangerous
muc.text: Check two: does it leak someone else's information, or say anything rude or dangerous?

muc.title: Citations
muc.text: Check three: does the answer have citations pointing to the right documents? With sources, customers can check for themselves.

muc.title: A person clicks confirm
muc.text: For real actions, like unlocking a card or sending money, AI only gets things ready. The user has to click confirm, and sometimes a staff member has to approve too. This is called human in the loop.

muc.title: Like airport security
muc.text: Together, the two gates are like airport security: scan on the way in, check on the way out. If one gate misses something, the other can still catch it.

muc.title: Ask for the link
muc.text: Next time a chatbot promises a refund or a discount, ask back: where is this policy written, send me the link. No link? Don't trust it yet.

muc.title: Will a new model break it?
muc.text: The guardrails are in place. But will switching to a new model break things? Part five: evaluation.
